title: Taming the ox
hook: picture five: patient discipline, the rope kept close (Ox-Herding 5)
tomorrow: why is the herder playing a flute on the way home?

segments.voice: Yesterday, it pulls: the ox caught, still straining toward the sweet grass. Picture five is what you do about that.

New job, new gym, new anything, and the first question in your head might be: what's the secret? A monk once brought that question to the Zen teacher Zhaozhou. I've just entered the monastery, he said. Please teach me. Zhaozhou asked: have you eaten your rice gruel? Yes, said the monk. Then wash your bowl. That's the whole exchange. It sounds like a brush-off. It isn't, and Zen kept it as a koan, in a collection called the Gateless Gate.
screen: `WHAT'S THE SECRET?` → `HAVE YOU EATEN?` → `THEN WASH YOUR BOWL.`

segments.voice: Kuoan's fifth picture says the same thing with a rope. The preface: when one thought rises, another follows right behind it. Things don't come from outside; they come from your own mind. So hold the nose-rope tight, and don't waver. The verse: keep whip and rope close, or the ox will wander off into the dust. Then the turn. Well tended, the ox grows gentle, and follows of its own accord, with no need for a tether. That's the Zen teaching about practice, named plainly: awakening isn't kept by one big moment. It's kept by daily, ordinary practice, the bowl washed every morning. Zhaozhou didn't hand the new monk a secret, because the bowl is the secret. In Zen, eating and cleaning are practice too, not breaks from it. And the rope isn't a punishment. It's how the ox learns the way home. Notice the end of the verse: the rope is held close so that one day it won't be needed. Discipline here is patient, plain and daily, and it's aiming at its own retirement.
screen: `ONE THOUGHT FOLLOWS ANOTHER.` · `KEEP THE ROPE CLOSE.` · `THE BOWL IS THE SECRET.` · `GENTLE, IT FOLLOWS UNTIED.` · then, large: `THE ROPE.`

segments.voice: If there's a cup or bowl nearby, wash it slowly, or just hold it and turn it in your hands, the way Zhaozhou's monk would after breakfast. Let the two minutes be that plain: one bowl, one rope, kept close.
Taming the ox: Kuoan's fifth picture. Patient discipline, the rope kept close until the ox walks on its own.
One to keep: the rope, daily and plain, held close until it isn't needed. Picture five, done.

howItsDone: In Zen, sitting, eating and cleaning are all treated as practice, done daily with attention. People on this path keep their own small daily rule, especially on busy days.
